Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
• Likely mild asthma exacerbation triggered by exercise and/or seasonal allergen exposure.  
  – Supporting: known asthma, new 2–3 day history of wheeze, dry cough, SOB; increased salbutamol use with poor relief; no infection signs.  
• Differential considerations (moderate): viral URTI precipitating flare; exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or sub-optimal inhaler technique.  
• Low-likelihood but noted: pulmonary embolism, community-acquired pneumonia (no systemic signs).  
• No current features suggesting life-threatening asthma, but safety-net given.

Management Plan
- Increase Clenil (beclomethasone) from 3 puffs BID to 4 puffs BID until reviewed.  
- Salbutamol inhaler up to every 2 hours PRN; seek emergency care if frequency remains this high or symptoms worsen.  
- Book urgent face-to-face GP appointment within next few days for chest exam, peak-flow, review of inhaler technique and control plan.  
- Advise A&E attendance if escalating breathlessness before review.  
- Discussed possible need for oral steroids/antibiotics depending on in-person findings.  
- No other interventions documented.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Asthma exacerbation – High likelihood: fits history of controlled asthma now symptomatic with wheeze/SOB, minimal reliever effect.  
2. Viral URTI–triggered asthma flare – Moderate likelihood: abrupt onset over days; common precipitant though no viral prodrome reported.  
3. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or poor inhaler technique – Moderate likelihood: onset during running, may contribute to loss of control.
